messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Call Center Agent
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Babies): Babies
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Vignette:
Lina, a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who had worked for years as a call center agent, came to treatment after months of trying to hold herself together at work and at home following the sudden death of her husband. She had been married for most of her adult life, and his loss had not felt like something that could be understood in ordinary terms because it came so quickly. One moment he was there in the rhythms of their shared life, and then he was gone, leaving her with the kind of unfinished ending she kept turning over in her mind. In the first days after his death, Lina moved through the practical tasks of arranging the funeral and receiving visitors almost mechanically, but even then she noticed that certain moments seemed to hit her with a force that made her body react before her thoughts could catch up. The funeral itself stayed with her as one of the most difficult experiences she had ever endured; later, cemeteries and anything resembling a memorial gathering would tighten her chest and make her feel as if she had stepped back into that first raw period of loss.

In the weeks that followed, Lina began to steer carefully around anything that might bring the grief rushing back. She stopped attending events where she might see people she had socialized with before her husband died, not because she disliked them, but because she dreaded being asked how she was doing and having to answer in a way that felt either too exposed or too false. She also found herself avoiding conversations about her husband or the circumstances of his death. If a relative started to ask what happened, she would change the subject, excuse herself, or give a brief answer and then go quiet. Anything that reminded her of him could unsettle her, so she became more careful in the everyday places of her life, trying not to linger over photographs, mementos, or familiar routines that made his absence feel immediate. At work, where she answered calls all day, she noticed that she could not concentrate as easily when something in the office reminded her of loss or when coworkers chatted about family events. She kept to herself more than she once had, and the distance grew gradually enough that she only fully noticed it when the invitations stopped coming.

Lina also described distressing moments when the event seemed to come back without warning, as if she had been dropped into it again. At times she would suddenly feel and act for a few seconds as though the terrible news were happening all over again, with the same abrupt jolt in her body and the same sense that she was not fully anchored in the present. These episodes were especially frightening because they arrived uninvited, in the middle of ordinary tasks. She might be at her desk at the call center, listening to a caller’s voice, when a wave of fear and horror would strike so sharply that she would need a moment to steady herself before continuing. She described a persistent background of strong negative feelings that were hard to contain: fear when she thought about the future without her husband, anger at the unfairness of how quickly he was taken, and guilt that she had not been able to do more, even though she knew on one level that the death had not been hers to prevent. At night, sleep became difficult. She would lie awake for long stretches, feeling tired but unable to settle, or wake after only a few hours and remain alert to the silence in the room. Over time, the broken sleep left her feeling worn down and more vulnerable the next day.

Her memory of the loss was not complete in the way she wished it could be. Lina found herself pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it, especially when she sensed the first stirrings of panic or sadness. Some moments were extremely clear to her—the shock of being told, the feeling of standing in the funeral home, the texture of certain voices—but other parts of the day were blank, as if her mind had gone dark around the edges. She was unsettled by the way fragments would appear suddenly without warning and then disappear again: a sight, a phrase, a glimpse of a face, a flash of the room where she first heard the news. These pieces did not come in order, and she could not make them stay long enough to form a full story, which left her feeling unsteady and frustrated with herself. She had hoped that time would make things easier, but instead the memories kept arriving in broken form, at unpredictable moments, and the reminders she encountered in the course of her job and daily life kept reopening the same wound.

By the time she sought help, Lina was not only grieving but exhausted by how carefully she had to move through her days. She had begun to worry that she was shrinking her life to keep from being overwhelmed, and she no longer felt comfortable with how much she was avoiding the people and places that once formed her ordinary world. What finally brought her in was the sense that she could no longer keep pretending that she was managing well. She hoped for relief from the sudden surges of fear and the sleepless nights, and she was most afraid that the memories would keep coming in pieces for the rest of her life, never allowing her to remember her husband in a way that felt whole.
